title: The Alpha Trap
summary: Start with a built five-item scale, add one near-duplicate item at a time, and watch Cronbach's alpha climb while the scale narrows and its correlation with a simulated outcome does not follow.
learningObjectives: Explain why Cronbach's alpha rises with both the number of items and their average intercorrelation, and why neither is a property of the construct.
Explain why a high alpha is not evidence of unidimensionality.
Explain why a high alpha is not evidence of validity, using the bloated specific factor as the mechanism.
Judge a scale on content coverage and item redundancy rather than on its reliability coefficient alone.
Recognise that a very high alpha in a short scale is a warning about item redundancy rather than a mark of quality.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout using native checkboxes, radios and buttons; the coverage chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible data table carrying the same numbers; state changes announced through the shell's polite live region; redundancy and outcome verdicts state their tone in words as well as by border colour; stage progress carried by aria-current and visible text; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths. The scale is a read-only list rather than a bank of checkboxes, and an item that repeats another's wording is marked by a left rule, a tinted ground and the printed words 'another way of asking ...', so the marking never rests on colour. Two buttons carry the whole interaction; the second appears only once there is something to drop. The readout gained a row for effective content areas, because the count of areas covered does not move while the scale narrows.
readmeTopic: Reliability: why a high Cronbach's alpha is not validity, unidimensionality or evidence of a good measure
itemSource: All 24 items were written for this tool. No published or commercial questionnaire is reproduced, in whole or in part.
simulationNotes: Every figure is the value implied by a fictional correlation model, not an estimate from a sample. Items load on a general factor, a content-area factor and, for near-duplicates, a wording-specific factor; the simulated outcome responds to the general factor and to breadth of coverage but not to wording. No sampling error is modelled, so no confidence intervals are shown. The construct and its five content areas are invented for teaching. From version 1.1.0 there is no item bank and no two-round build. The learner is given a five-item scale - one distinct item from each of the five content areas, alpha 0.684, just below the 0.70 a reviewer would ask for - and the only move is to add one of five paraphrases of a single item, one at a time. The model-implied sequence is alpha 0.684, 0.711, 0.753, 0.793, 0.826, 0.852; correlation with the simulated outcome 0.573, 0.581, 0.574, 0.562, 0.549, 0.536; effective content areas 5.00, 4.50, 3.77, 3.20, 2.79, 2.50. The count of areas covered stays at five throughout, which is why the readout also reports effective content areas, the inverse Simpson index over the area proportions. The first addition raises the outcome correlation slightly and every later one lowers it, so the lesson is not that items should never be added. Dropping the repeats returns the scale to six items, alpha 0.711 and the highest outcome correlation anywhere in the model, which is the counter-argument stated as a comparison rather than as a second round.
